nature-eco-454.title: Fringing, barrier, atoll: the shapes of coral reefs
nature-eco-454.text: An atoll is a ring of reef around a lagoon with no island in the middle, and it usually began as a reef around a volcanic island. Coral reefs are classed by shape and setting, classically as fringing reefs, barrier reefs and atolls, with platform reefs often added. A fringing reef is attached to the shore or separated from it by a narrow, shallow channel. A barrier reef is separated from the shore by a deep channel or lagoon. Platform reefs grow wherever the seabed rises near enough to the surface for reef-building corals.

nature-eco-501.title: Life on the ocean's skin
nature-eco-501.text: Some snails spend their lives floating at the very top of the sea. They belong to the neuston, the community of organisms that live at the ocean's surface, along with drifting Sargassum seaweed. This marine surface ecosystem matters more than its thinness suggests. Many ecologically and economically important fish species are part of the neuston or depend on it. The surface is also on the front line of climate change and pollution.

nature-eco-504.title: River ecosystems: water that drains the land
nature-eco-504.text: Fast, turbulent water carries more dissolved oxygen than a slow pool, and it supports more species. A river ecosystem is a flowing-water, or lotic, ecosystem that drains the landscape, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions. Each river is part of a larger watershed, where small headwater streams feed ever larger channels. Food sources change along the way. Streams under a forest canopy get most of their food from trees, while wider, open streams get most from algae. Threats include water loss, dams, chemical pollution and introduced species. Dams cut spring floods and trap sediment, harming wetlands downstream.

nature-eco-482.title: Riparian zones: the green strip along a river
nature-eco-482.text: The name comes from the Latin ripa, meaning river bank. A riparian zone is the strip where land meets a river or stream, with its own water-loving vegetation. Such strips also go by names such as buffer zones and corridors. They work as natural filters, shielding waters from excess sediment, polluted runoff and erosion. Buffer zones can cut nitrate pollution from manure and fertilizer washing off farm fields, and riparian zones that are also wetlands remove nitrate especially well. Riparian plants give shelter and food to many aquatic animals, and their shade limits swings in stream temperature. Because they support so many species, these strips are often protected under national plans for wildlife. Some are natural; others are engineered to hold soil or restore damaged land. Land beside a watercourse that stays waterlogged for a season or more is usually called a wetland instead, because of its hydric soils, soils formed under saturation.

nature-eco-462.title: Floodplains: the land a river borrows
nature-eco-462.text: The Nile and Mississippi basins grew farms and cities on land their rivers regularly reclaim. A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that floods when the river runs high. Regular floods deposit nutrients, so floodplain soils are often very fertile. People have settled there to use that rich soil and fresh water, and the risk of flooding has led to growing efforts to control floods. Floodplains support diverse, productive and often very species-rich ecosystems. Floodplain forests protect waterways from erosion and pollution and soften the impact of floodwaters. Yet the main ways people destroy floodplain ecosystems are flood control itself, reservoirs for hydroelectric power, and conversion to farmland.

nature-eco-443.title: How wetlands soak up floods
nature-eco-443.text: Walling a river in can make its floods worse. Floodplains and other wetlands act as natural storage reservoirs that soak up excess water and so reduce flooding downstream. They work in several ways. River floodplains let floodwater spread over a wide area, which lowers its depth and speed. Headwater wetlands, high in a river's catchment, slow rain runoff and snowmelt so they do not rush straight into rivers, which helps prevent sudden floods. During heavy rain, wetlands hold the extra water, reducing the area, depth and duration of flooding. Remove that storage and the system changes. Draining floodplains or hemming rivers in with levees forces the same rain through a narrower channel. Flood peaks then get higher and arrive faster. A wetland controls floods by giving water room; take the room away and the peaks rise.

nature-eco-464.title: Floodplain ecology: life timed to the flood pulse
nature-eco-464.text: Many river fish spawn just as the flood begins, using the newly flooded river edge, and their young must grow fast before the water falls. Floodplain ecology centres on this flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain. Floods bring in nutrient-rich debris and release nutrients from the soil they cover. Floodplain plants and animals grow and die fast, which lets them colonise shifting ground, and floodplain trees are fast-growing. Away from the river, plant zones follow a gradient of soil moisture, oxygen and flood frequency. Floodplain forests covered 1% of Europe in the 1800s, and because they were cleared less than other forests, they are important refuges for biodiversity. Flood control sharpens the boundary between water and land, which reduces habitat diversity.

nature-eco-507.title: When water ecosystems are pushed too far
nature-eco-507.text: The Great Lakes show how pollution, over-harvesting and invasive species can combine. Threats to aquatic ecosystems are the stresses that degrade them once they exceed what the ecosystem can absorb. Stresses can be physical, such as changes in temperature, flow or light. They can be chemical: nutrients, oxygen-consuming materials and toxins. Or they can be biological, like over-harvesting and exotic species. Human-driven climate change disrupts where plants and animals live and has hurt deep-sea biodiversity, coastal fish and coral reefs. Even human-made waters such as ditches and fish-farm ponds trade biodiversity for their intended purpose.

nature-eco-548.title: Large marine ecosystems: managing the sea by region
nature-eco-548.text: There are 66 large marine ecosystems, contributing an estimated $3 trillion a year and 90% of the world's annual marine fish catch. A large marine ecosystem is an ocean region of roughly 200,000 km2 or more, defined by its seabed shape, water movement, productivity and linked food webs. The US agency NOAA developed the concept in 1984. Its aim was to guide conservation and shared management of whole ecosystems across national borders.

nature-eco-472.title: Planting trees on grasslands: a contested fix
nature-eco-472.text: A map by the {{ref:nature-hist-032}} and the IUCN, showing 2 billion hectares for restoring forests, was criticised for including 900 million hectares of grasslands. Planting trees on grasslands, often to store carbon, can damage grasslands and the services they provide. Critics say tree-planting campaigns target grasslands and savannas where forests would not naturally grow. Restoration focused on forests risks misclassifying grassland as degraded forest, which helps make grasslands the least protected biome. Grasslands and savannas benefit people too, and they are not meant to be forests.

nature-eco-473.title: Fire and grazing: keeping grasslands open
nature-eco-473.text: Reserves in Brazil that banned fire and grazing were quickly taken over by shrubs. Many grasslands depend on disturbances such as fire and grazing to stay open, so how they are managed can make them persist or vanish. Grazing and fire keep woody plants from invading. In Brazilian highland grasslands, areas without the traditional burning every two years and cattle grazing could disappear within 30 years. Not everyone agrees on how far grasslands depend on fire and grazing, and the question remains controversial.

nature-eco-469.title: Semi-natural grasslands: wild meadows kept by people
nature-eco-469.text: A meadow in Estonia held a European record of 76 plant species in a single square meter. It was a semi-natural grassland: one with wild, unsown plant communities, kept open by human activities such as grazing and mowing. These grasslands can be extremely species-rich. Almost 90% of Europe's semi-natural grasslands disappeared during the 20th century, for political and economic reasons. Fertilizing and re-sowing them for farming usually leaves few wild plants. To save what remains, conservation groups buy these grasslands or pay landowners grants to manage them appropriately.

nature-eco-468.title: Prairie, pampas, steppe: kinds of grassland
nature-eco-468.text: During the Pleistocene ice ages, a cold, dry 'mammoth steppe' grassland covered much of the Northern Hemisphere. Today grasslands are grouped by climate and setting into broad types: tropical, temperate, flooded, montane, tundra and desert grasslands. Tropical and subtropical grasslands and savannas get 90 to 150 centimeters of rain a year and support grazers like wildebeest and zebra. Temperate grasslands include the North American prairie, the Pampas and the European steppes, home to large herbivores such as bison. Flooded grasslands such as the Everglades and the Pantanal are under water seasonally or all year.

nature-eco-483.title: What riverside strips do for people
nature-eco-483.text: A shaded stream stays cool; thin out the trees along its banks and its temperature climbs and swings, sometimes enough to kill fish. Riparian zones provide many such benefits, from slowing floods and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation. River bends, plants and roots slow the water, which reduces soil erosion and flood damage. Trapped sediment leaves the water clearer and builds the banks. The strips serve as wildlife corridors, letting aquatic and riverside organisms move along rivers instead of living in isolated groups. They also raise nearby property values through views and amenity, and make room for fishing, swimming and boating.

nature-eco-484.title: Leaving buffers when forests are logged
nature-eco-484.text: Logging next to a stream can fill it with sediment, change its species and pollute its water. Riparian buffers in logging mean leaving the riverside strip undisturbed during timber harvesting so it keeps protecting the stream. The untouched soil and vegetation give shade, leaf litter and wood, and hold back soil eroding from the logged area. How well a buffer works depends on soil type, root structure, climate and plant cover.

nature-eco-485.title: Repairing damaged riverbanks
nature-eco-485.text: Clearing land and then flooding can quickly strip a riverbank of grasses and soil. Riparian zone restoration repairs such damage by removing human structures, by active rehabilitation, or simply by giving the bank time. Methods range from erosion control and replanting to log sills, rock placement and short barriers jutting into the stream ({{ref:nature-nbs-056}}), plus invasive species control. Fast-growing pioneer 'weeds' can kick-start succession, holding soil until trees and grasses return. Conservationists urge that the value of riparian ecosystem services be written into management plans, where it has usually been left out.

nature-eco-564.title: Rainforest layers: from dark floor to emergent crowns
nature-eco-564.text: Only 2% of the sunlight reaches a rainforest floor, so only low-light plants grow there. Rainforests are organised into vertical layers, from forest floor and understory to canopy and emergent layer, each with its own community of plants and animals. The canopy forms a roof over the lower layers and contains most of the largest trees, typically 30–45 m tall. Emergent trees rise above it to 45–55 m, occasionally 70–80 m. Only this top layer is unique to tropical rainforests.

nature-eco-465.title: Living with floods on the floodplain
nature-eco-465.text: River floods, especially on China's Yellow River, have been among the deadliest natural disasters, led by the 1931 China floods. Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works that limit flood damage to floodplain residents. How far a floodplain floods depends on the size of the flood, expressed as a return period, such as the 100-year flood with a one-in-a-hundred chance each year. In the United States, a national program offers {{ref:nature-clim-039}} for properties in flood-prone areas drawn on risk maps. Yet upstream development such as a large car park can raise flood levels, and the maps are rarely updated. Some towns have been moved off floodplains. Elsewhere annual floods are part of the rural economy, supporting recessional agriculture: planting as the water recedes.

nature-eco-463.title: How rivers build their floodplains
nature-eco-463.text: A meandering river eats away the outside of each bend and builds a sandbar, a point bar, on the inside, slowly laying down a level floodplain. Most floodplains are built this way, by rivers depositing sediment both inside their bends and when floods spill over the banks. Water spilling over the banks drops a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel. Over time this forms natural levees, low ridges along the river's edge. In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

nature-eco-466.title: Floodplains as phosphorus traps
nature-eco-466.text: Much of the phosphorus in fresh water comes from wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff, and too much of it is a problem. Floodplains can store phosphorus in their soils and plants, keeping it from overloading rivers downstream. Floodplain forests act as phosphorus sinks. Cutting rivers off from their floodplains removes that sink and worsens the overload.

nature-eco-434.title: Mosquito ditching: a cure that bred more mosquitoes
nature-eco-434.text: In the early 20th century people dug straight ditches through salt marshes, believing that draining them would reduce mosquitoes. It backfired. The ditches destroyed habitat for killifish, small fish that eat mosquitoes, so mosquito numbers actually rose and wading birds lost food. The ditches are still visible despite efforts to refill them.

nature-eco-432.title: Too much nitrogen in salt marshes
nature-eco-432.text: Salt marsh plants are normally short of nitrogen, so adding more reshuffles which species win. Nitrogen loading is the extra nitrogen from sewage, urban runoff and farm and industrial waste that flows into salt marshes and changes their plant life. Disturbed marshes can be invaded by the aggressive reed Phragmites australis, which crowds out native plants and harms insects and birds too.

nature-eco-429.title: How a mudflat becomes a salt marsh
nature-eco-429.text: A salt marsh begins as bare tidal mud. It forms when that mud builds up with sediment until tides flood them less often, letting plants take root. Rivers slow down as they reach the flat tidal zone and drop their sediment, helped by the rising tide. Pioneer plants, the first to arrive, catch more sediment around their stems, forming mounds that join into raised terraces bound by roots. As the surface rises, flooding gets shorter and shallower, and a succession of plant communities moves in.

nature-eco-431.title: Reclaiming salt marsh for farmland
nature-eco-431.text: In one English estuary, abandoned reclaimed land saw little vegetation return in 60–75 years, because the ground was too low and compacted. Land reclamation turned salt marsh into dry farmland, often by building dikes that kept the tide out. It changed vegetation, sediment, salinity and water flow, caused biodiversity loss and added nutrients. Once done, the damage can last for decades.

nature-eco-435.title: Salt marsh restoration: bringing back the tide
nature-eco-435.text: Once seen as wasteland, salt marshes are now recognised as among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivalling tropical rainforests. Salt marsh restoration brings damaged or reclaimed marshes back toward their natural state, a practice that has grown since the 1980s. Many countries now protect marshes by law; the US {{ref:nature-pol-155}} and the EU Habitats Directive give them strong protection. Restoration can use {{ref:nature-nbs-040}}, letting the sea back onto reclaimed land, or reclaim land for marsh, either leaving a site to recover naturally or actively rebuilding the habitat. Natural recovery can take 2–10 years or longer. Replanting native vegetation speeds it up and usually works better. Effective restoration takes considerable time and effort and needs careful long-term monitoring. Not everywhere has changed course. Fast-growing coastal populations in parts of Asia still tend to ignore marsh value and keep reclaiming the land.

nature-eco-436.title: The microbes that run a salt marsh
nature-eco-436.text: In salt marsh mud, bacteria that breathe sulfate instead of oxygen can account for up to 50% of the breakdown of organic matter. Microbes do most of the nutrient cycling and chemical processing in salt marshes, thriving in the salty, low-oxygen mud. These sulfate-reducing bacteria help recycle nutrients and reduce nitrate pollution. Cyanobacteria are important nitrogen fixers, turning nitrogen from the air into a usable form and supplying it to diatoms and other microalgae.

nature-eco-551.title: How a forest stand grows old
nature-eco-551.text: A forest stand, a patch of trees growing together, ages in stages. After a disturbance that replaces it, it passes through stand initiation, stem exclusion and understory reinitiation before reaching old growth. In stem exclusion, trees compete for light: slow growers die and canopies close, so only very shade-tolerant plants survive beneath. In understory reinitiation, scattered tree deaths open gaps that let shade-tolerant species establish below. In old growth, canopy trees die at different times, so trees beneath grow at different stages and rates, giving a mixed-age stand. Such stands are more stable, because a uniformly aged climax stand degrades fairly quickly into a new cycle of succession.

nature-eco-552.title: Old growth through a logger's eyes
nature-eco-552.text: To a logging company, an old-growth stand is one past the economic best age for harvesting, usually 80 to 150 years depending on species. Old-growth forests were often logged first. They held the most valuable timber, were thought at risk of rot or pests, and occupied land wanted for faster-growing second growth. Their large trees have been aggressively logged worldwide, causing many conflicts between logging companies and environmental groups. Old growth is not always the most profitable timber, though. Coastal British Columbia is shifting harvests to younger second-growth stands.
